section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the word "Midbar" (desert) relates to speech uttered in self-nullification, which brings about "Sinai" (hatred for the nations) and empowers the Nefesh HaElokis while providing strength to the Nefesh HaBahamis.
section.t: And this is [the meaning of] "In the third month... on this day they came to the desert of Sinai,"
"Desert" (Midbar) is from the term "speech" (dibur),
and it is called "Midbar" with the addition of the letter Mem, to indicate that the speech is in a state of self-nullification, like one who answers after the caller
(as explained at length in the discourses),
and through this, Sinai is brought about, [meaning] that hatred descended upon the nations of the world.
For when the study of Torah is in a state of self-nullification, then it becomes
(strength for the Nefesh HaElokis and)
a resource (tushiyah) for the Nefesh HaBahamis,
for "hatred descended upon the nations of the world" includes also the body and the Nefesh HaBahamis.
[And one should note the teaching of the Baal Shem Tov
on the verse,
"When you see the donkey of your enemy,"
when you look with good contemplation at your material, which is the body,
you will see that it is your enemy,
for it hates the soul.]

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses how after the state of "Refidim" (weakness in Torah study), one travels away from this weakness through the service of "Midbar," arriving at Sinai with greater strength.
section.t: Afterwards, the verse says, "And they journeyed from Refidim,"
Refidim is so named because they loosened their hands from words of Torah,
meaning that he is not opposed to Torah; on the contrary, he studies Torah,
but his study is with laxity and weakness,
and through the service of "Midbar" (desert/speech of nullification), he moves himself
(also)
from the laxity and weakness in words of Torah and does repentance
for this.
And the verse continues
(after it says "and they journeyed from Refidim")
"and they came to the desert of Sinai... before the mountain,"
for this that he was initially in Refidim brings him to strengthen himself
in words of Torah even more.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that through studying this Torah passage now, there is an added empowerment for "journeying from Refidim," especially on Tu B'Shvat, which provides special strength for Torah study, mitzvos, and exalted repentance leading to the true and complete redemption.
section.t: And 4)
One could say,
that through studying this verse now,
the empowerment for "and they journeyed from Refidim" is even greater.
For the first time,
the empowerment for "and they journeyed from Refidim" was through the completion of the preparation for the Giving of the Torah on Rosh Chodesh Sivan,
and now,
there is also the empowerment from the Giving of the Torah in past years,
and from the study of Torah after the Giving of the Torah, through which additional strength is added to the matter of the Giving of the Torah
(as above, section 6).
And especially since we are on the fifteenth day of the month, when the moon is in its fullness,
and within this itself—on the fifteenth of Shevat,
the New Year for the Tree,
which relates to a good and spacious land—there is a special empowerment to increase in Torah study and in the fulfillment of mitzvos in a manner of "a good and spacious land,"
and likewise regarding repentance
("and they journeyed from Refidim")
that it should be in a manner of "a good and spacious land,"
meaning supernal repentance, which is with great joy,
and when Israel repents, they are immediately redeemed,
"and you shall be gathered one by one, O children of Israel,"
that the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself
brings them to a good and spacious land literally,
in the true and complete redemption through our righteous Mashiach,
speedily, truly.
